title: SC-500 distinctions
_note: Cards are distinctions, not definitions. Each front is a question the exam asks by implication; each back is the shortest true answer. 'module' points at the file that teaches it properly. Scheduling is Leitner: 1, 3, 7, 16, 35 days.

cards.front: PIM: eligible versus active
cards.back: Eligible means the role must be activated, with whatever the role setting demands - MFA, justification, a ticket, approval. Active means it is held now. Eligibility is what makes standing privilege unnecessary.

cards.front: Which PIM settings live on the role, and which on the assignment?
cards.back: Activation maximum duration, MFA, justification, approval and notifications are role settings. Start and end dates and the eligible-or-active choice are per assignment.

cards.front: Two Conditional Access policies apply: one grants, one blocks. Outcome?
cards.back: Blocked. Every applicable policy is evaluated on every sign-in, there is no priority ordering, and block wins over any number of grants.

cards.front: App registration, enterprise application, service principal
cards.back: The app registration is the application object in its home tenant. The enterprise application is the service principal - the instance of that app in a tenant. Permissions are granted to the service principal.

cards.front: Delegated versus application permission
cards.back: Delegated acts on behalf of a signed-in user and is capped by that user's own access. Application acts without a user and is capped only by the permission itself - which is why it requires admin consent.

cards.front: System-assigned versus user-assigned managed identity
cards.back: System-assigned is tied to one resource and deleted with it. User-assigned is its own resource, shared across resources and surviving their deletion.

cards.front: The workload is not in Azure. Which identity?
cards.back: Workload identity federation. A managed identity only exists for Azure resources, and an app registration with a stored secret moves the credential rather than removing it.

cards.front: Key Vault: RBAC or access policy?
cards.back: One model per vault, not both. RBAC is the current recommendation, scopable to an individual secret and visible in the normal role assignment surface. Access policies are vault-wide lists.

cards.front: Key Vault soft delete versus purge protection
cards.back: Soft delete is always on and cannot be turned off. Purge protection is opt-in and cannot be turned off once enabled - it blocks permanent deletion until the retention period expires.

cards.front: Defender for Key Vault versus Defender CSPM secrets scanning
cards.back: Defender for Key Vault alerts on anomalous access to the vault. CSPM secrets scanning finds credentials sitting in code and on disks - outside the vault entirely.

cards.front: Does subscription Owner grant access to secrets?
cards.back: No. Management-plane roles do not carry data-plane access - though an Owner can grant it to themselves, which is why the assignment is the thing to audit.

cards.front: Azure Policy effects worth knowing cold
cards.back: audit reports, deny blocks creation, modify changes the request, deployIfNotExists deploys a remediation afterwards, append adds a field. Only deny stops the resource existing.

cards.front: Policy exemption versus exclusion scope
cards.back: An exclusion removes a scope from the assignment entirely. An exemption keeps it in scope but records a justified, expiring waiver - so it stays visible in compliance reporting.

cards.front: CanNotDelete versus ReadOnly locks
cards.back: CanNotDelete allows changes but not deletion. ReadOnly blocks changes too, and breaks more than expected because some read operations are implemented as POST. Both inherit downward.

cards.front: Does a lock protect the data inside a resource?
cards.back: No. Locks are management plane. Blobs in a locked storage account are untouched by it - that is blob soft delete, versioning or an immutability policy.

cards.front: Entra role versus Azure RBAC role
cards.back: Entra roles govern the directory; Azure RBAC governs ARM resources. Global Administrator grants nothing in Azure until someone uses the elevate access toggle, which assigns User Access Administrator at root scope.

cards.front: The three parts of a custom Azure role
cards.back: Actions and NotActions - or DataActions and NotDataActions for the data plane - and AssignableScopes, which limits where the definition can be used at all.

cards.front: Protecting backups from a rogue administrator
cards.back: Multi-user authorization with a Resource Guard: a critical operation needs a second principal to approve. Soft delete and immutable vault settings harden the data; MUA is what assumes the admin is the threat.

cards.front: Four ways to authorize access to blob data
cards.back: Entra identity with a data role, account key, SAS, or anonymous public access. Setting AllowSharedKeyAccess to false removes the second and forces the first.

cards.front: Revoke one issued service SAS without breaking the others
cards.back: Only if it references a stored access policy - revoke or edit the policy. Otherwise the only lever is rotating the account key, which invalidates everything signed with it.

cards.front: User delegation SAS: what makes it different?
cards.back: It is signed with Entra credentials rather than the account key, so it inherits the identity's permissions and is revoked by revoking the delegation key or the role assignment.

cards.front: Trusted services exception versus resource instance rule
cards.back: The exception admits a whole class of Microsoft services. A resource instance rule names one specific resource. Narrower is the exam-correct answer whenever both would work.

cards.front: Setting an Entra admin on a SQL server - is that enough?
cards.back: No. SQL logins still exist and Conditional Access cannot see them. Entra-only authentication is the second step, and it disables SQL authentication including the original admin.

cards.front: TDE, Always Encrypted, dynamic data masking
cards.back: TDE protects files and backups at rest and is transparent to queries. Always Encrypted keeps keys off the server so administrators cannot read the column. Masking hides results and is not a security boundary.

cards.front: Auditing enabled at both server and database level
cards.back: Both policies run side by side. You get duplicate records, duplicate ingestion cost and duplicate rows in every query - the fix is to pick one level.

cards.front: NSG default rules
cards.back: Inbound: VNet allowed, Azure Load Balancer allowed, everything else denied. Outbound: VNet and internet allowed, everything else denied. First match by priority wins, lowest number first.

cards.front: What an application security group actually is
cards.back: A named grouping of NICs that NSG rules can reference as a source or destination, so rules are written by role rather than by address range.

cards.front: Virtual Network Manager security admin rules
cards.back: Evaluated before NSGs, from a management scope above the VNets. Allow lets the NSG still decide; Deny and AlwaysAllow cannot be overridden by a subscription owner - which is the whole point.

cards.front: Azure Firewall rule processing order
cards.back: DNAT, then network rules, then application rules, within rule collection groups ordered by priority. A network rule match means application rules never run - which silently defeats FQDN rules.

cards.front: Can an NSG filter by FQDN?
cards.back: No. An NSG knows addresses, ports, protocols and service tags. FQDN filtering is Azure Firewall; HTTP inspection is WAF.

cards.front: Network Watcher: effective security rules versus IP flow verify
cards.back: Effective rules flatten every NSG applying to a NIC into one list. IP flow verify tests one specific flow and names the rule that decided it.

cards.front: Service endpoint versus private endpoint
cards.back: A service endpoint extends the subnet's identity to the service over the backbone - still a public endpoint, no private IP, no on-premises access. A private endpoint is a NIC with a private IP mapped to one resource.

cards.front: Two things a private endpoint does not do by itself
cards.back: It does not disable the public endpoint - that is a separate setting - and it does not fix name resolution without the privatelink DNS zone linked to the VNet.

cards.front: Private Link service
cards.back: The provider side: you publish your own service behind a Standard Load Balancer so consumers can reach it through their own private endpoints, including across tenants.

cards.front: Service endpoint policy
cards.back: Narrows a service endpoint from 'this subnet may reach the service' to 'and only these specific accounts'. It is the exfiltration control for service endpoints.

cards.front: Microsoft Entra Private Access
cards.back: Identity-centric access to private applications through connectors, part of Global Secure Access. A user-to-app control, not a VNet networking feature.

cards.front: Purview DSPM for AI answers which question?
cards.back: What sensitive data is flowing into and out of AI, and which content is overshared to Copilot. It is a data-layer discovery surface, not a runtime detection.

cards.front: Defender for AI services answers which question?
cards.back: Is someone jailbreaking, poisoning or exfiltrating through our Azure-hosted models. It builds on Content Safety Prompt Shields plus threat intelligence and sends alerts into Defender XDR.

cards.front: Foundry guardrails answer which question?
cards.back: Should this prompt or response be permitted at all. Content filters, Prompt Shields and blocklists act at the model layer - they block, where Defender alerts.

cards.front: AI gateway in API Management answers which question?
cards.back: Who may call the model, how much may they spend, and is traffic inspected, cached and logged centrally. Policies: llm-token-limit, llm-emit-token-metric, llm-content-safety, llm-semantic-cache-lookup and -store.

cards.front: One application is consuming the whole model quota
cards.back: llm-token-limit in API Management, keyed per consumer - and the traffic has to route through the gateway for it to mean anything.

cards.front: Entra Agent ID
cards.back: A first-class identity for an agent, so it can be governed like an account: Conditional Access, ownership, lifecycle, and blast-radius analysis in Defender XDR.

cards.front: Conditional Access for agents on Microsoft 365 E5 - what is missing?
cards.back: Additional agent licensing beyond Entra ID P1/P2. E5 supplies neither, so this is a procurement decision before it is a configuration one. Verify the current position; this area moves.

cards.front: Blast radius analysis
cards.back: Defender XDR, for Entra Agent ID - what a compromised agent could reach. It requires the agent to carry an agent identity, which is why governance comes first.

cards.front: Trusted launch: what does it add?
cards.back: Secure boot and vTPM, enabling boot integrity and attestation. It is a security type chosen at VM creation, and integrity monitoring builds on it.

cards.front: Bastion versus just-in-time VM access
cards.back: Bastion removes the public IP by brokering RDP/SSH over TLS to a private address. JIT removes the standing allow rule by opening the port only on an approved, time-bound request. Different halves; they compose.

cards.front: Why onboard to Azure Arc before enabling Defender for Servers?
cards.back: Arc makes the machine an Azure resource, so it can carry policy, inventory, machine configuration and free recommendations. Only then is paying for a plan a decision made with visibility.

cards.front: Agentless scanning versus the agent
cards.back: Agentless snapshots the disk through cloud APIs - broad coverage, no install, no runtime cost, point-in-time. The agent gives live detection and response. They answer different questions.

cards.front: Azure Machine Configuration
cards.back: Audits and enforces in-guest settings on Azure and Arc-enabled machines through policy. The successor to guest configuration; it needs the extension and a managed identity.

cards.front: Defender for Containers covers which two phases?
cards.back: Posture - registry and cluster misconfiguration, image vulnerability findings - and runtime threat detection on the cluster. Hardening recommendations sit on the posture side.

cards.front: Azure Functions: which control answers 'only authenticated callers'?
cards.back: App Service authentication - Easy Auth - in front of the function, plus network access restrictions or private endpoints. Function keys are not an authentication system.

cards.front: WAF on Application Gateway versus on Front Door
cards.back: Application Gateway is regional and sits in front of a regional back end. Front Door is global, and Premium adds Private Link origins so the origin can stay off the public internet.

cards.front: Recommendation, attack path, alert - which costs what?
cards.back: Recommendations are free foundational CSPM. Attack paths need Defender CSPM. Alerts need the workload protection plan for that resource type. The noun in the stem gives you the answer.

cards.front: What is uniquely EASM?
cards.back: Internet-facing assets you did not know you owned. Defender CSPM reasons over your inventory; EASM finds what is not in it. Look for 'unknown' or 'unmanaged'.

cards.front: Connecting AWS or GCP to Defender for Cloud
cards.back: A multicloud connector per account or project, which brings those resources into CSPM and lets workload plans extend to them. Not a matter of agents alone.

cards.front: Sentinel Reader, Responder, Contributor
cards.back: Reader views. Responder adds incident management - assign, reclassify, close. Contributor can create and edit analytics rules. Analysts get Responder, not Contributor.

cards.front: Who can author a playbook?
cards.back: Whoever holds the Logic App permissions, because that is what a playbook is. Sentinel Playbook Operator only lists, views and runs them.

cards.front: AMA plus DCR versus Windows Event Forwarding
cards.back: AMA with a DCR collects from machines you can install on. WEF forwards events to a collector that runs AMA, with the DCR reading the forwarded events channel - for machines you cannot touch.

cards.front: Where is it decided what a machine collects?
cards.back: In the data collection rule, not on the agent and not in the workspace. That is the change the Log Analytics agent retirement forced.

cards.front: Syslog and CEF collection shape
cards.back: Appliances send to a Linux forwarder running AMA; the DCR selects facilities and severities, and CEF is parsed into its own table. The forwarder is the part people forget to secure.

cards.front: Automation rule versus playbook
cards.back: An automation rule is the trigger and condition logic inside Sentinel - assign, tag, close, or call a playbook. The playbook is the Logic App that does the external work.

cards.front: Sentinel analytics tier versus data lake tier
cards.back: Analytics is interactive, and analytics rules and hunting run on it. The lake is cheap long-horizon storage queried by search jobs. Moving a table to the lake stops real-time detection on it.

cards.front: Cutting Sentinel cost: ingestion or retention?
cards.back: Different problems. Ingestion is reduced by a DCR transformation or a cheaper tier for a noisy source. Retention is tiering and retention settings. Confusing them breaks a detection or an audit.

cards.front: Shortening total retention - is it immediate?
cards.back: No. Microsoft waits 30 days before removing data, so a mistaken change can be reverted. Increasing retention applies to data already ingested and not yet removed.

cards.front: Security Copilot: what is the unit and why does it matter?
cards.back: Security Compute Units, provisioned as capacity that bills whether or not you prompt it. In a lab it is the single largest budget risk - smallest capacity, short bursts, deprovision immediately.
